title: IGrasp: your first IPC command, from Rust to the mock to the UI
intro: You will add one command to IGrasp end to end. You will write the Rust handler and its ts-rs types, register it in lib.rs, declare it on the Backend interface, implement it twice (tauri.ts and the in-memory mock), and call it from a store and a view. You will also know which checks catch a missed step, and which ones don't.
subject: Your first contribution: adding a new IPC command from Rust to the mock backend and the UI
docsNote: No page lists the places a new command must touch. The checklist lives in the agent-oriented notes and is only implied by ADR 0007 and the command table in docs/architecture.md; a short "Adding an IPC command" section in CONTRIBUTING.md would help.

chapters.title: The map: one command, five places
chapters.goal: Name every file a new command touches (commands/*.rs, lib.rs, ipc/types.ts, ipc/tauri.ts, ipc/mock/index.ts, a store) by following get_graph_status through them, and explain why src/ipc/client.ts is the single switch between the real backend and the mock.
chapters.hootIntro: Before you write a line, let's trace get_graph_status through every file a new IGrasp command has to touch.

steps.title: A command is one name spelled in five files
steps.body: A command has no registry that generates the others: `get_graph_status` is typed by hand in the Rust handler (`commands/graph.rs`), the `generate_handler!` list (`lib.rs`), the `Backend` interface (`ipc/types.ts`), `tauriBackend` (`ipc/tauri.ts`) and the mock (`ipc/mock/index.ts`). A sixth place, a zustand store, is where the UI actually calls it. The snake_case string in `invoke('get_graph_status')` is the only link between the Rust and TypeScript halves, so a typo there is a runtime error, not a compile error.

sources.why: The command table lists get_graph_status among the IPC commands.

stops.annotation: The Rust end. `with_graph` takes the workspace read lock via `with_workspace`, so with no folder open the command fails with `AppError::NoRootOpen`. The handler itself is one line: `g.status(generation)`.
`tauri::generate_handler!` is the allow-list of callable commands. A `#[tauri::command]` function missing here compiles fine and is simply unreachable from the webview.

The contract. `getGraphStatus(): Promise<GraphStatus>` sits in `Backend` next to the other graph queries, with the generated `GraphStatus` type imported at the top of the file (line 20) and re-exported (line 68).
The real implementation is a one-liner over the local `invoke` wrapper. Arguments are camelCase objects (`{ relPath }`) matching the Rust parameter names, which Tauri converts from snake_case.

The mock re-implements the same rule in TypeScript: reject with `NoRootOpen` when `state.root` is null, then answer from `state.graph` and `state.index`, with `ready` false until the fake build finishes.

The caller. `loadStatus` imports `backend` from `ipc/client`, remembers the generation before the await, and drops the answer if the generation moved on. Conventions say IPC calls live in stores, not components.

steps.caption: Stores see only `Backend`; client.ts picks which implementation sits behind it. Only the left branch crosses the process boundary.

sources.why: The Backend interface both sides implement.
The Rust end of the call.

steps.title: client.ts is the only switch
steps.body: `select()` returns `tauriBackend` when `'__TAURI_INTERNALS__' in window`, otherwise it builds the mock and publishes its controls on `window.__igraspMock`. The choice is made once, at module load, and exported as the constant `backend`, so no store or component ever branches on the environment. The cost: `tauri.ts` is imported even in the browser (its comment says it is unused there, with window calls resolved lazily by `win()`), and a bundle in the wrong environment cannot swap implementations at runtime. The gain is that Vitest, `npm run dev` and Playwright exercise the exact same store code as the desktop app.

sources.why: isTauri, select and the exported backend.
Lazy window access because the module is imported outside Tauri.

steps.title: Spot the environment test
steps.prompt: Click the line that decides, at runtime, that the app is running inside the Tauri webview.
steps.explanation: `isTauri()` looks for `__TAURI_INTERNALS__` on `window`. `select()` uses it on line 13 to return `tauriBackend`; everything else gets the mock, with its controls exposed for tests on line 15.

steps.question: You add `getFoo()` to the `Backend` interface and implement it in `tauriBackend` and the mock, but forget to list the Rust command in `generate_handler!` in lib.rs. What happens?
choices: tsc and Vitest pass; the call fails only when the real app invokes it
The TypeScript build fails on the unknown command name
cargo test fails because the command is unregistered
The mock throws, since it checks lib.rs at startup
steps.hint: Which of these checks ever reads the string passed to `invoke`?
steps.explanation: The command name is a plain string in `tauri.ts`, and the mock never touches lib.rs, so typecheck and unit tests are green. Only a run of the real app (or a manual check) reveals the missing handler. Omitting a method from either implementation, by contrast, is caught by `tsc`: `tauriBackend` is typed `Backend` and the mock returns `Backend & { controls }`.

sources.why: The handler list that must be extended by hand.
The mock's return type is Backend & { controls }.

steps.title: Match the file to its job
steps.prompt: Match each file to what it does for a command.

pairs.right: The #[tauri::command] handler and the response structs
The generate_handler! list that exposes the command
The Backend interface and re-exports of generated types
The real implementation over invoke, with error mapping
The in-memory implementation used in browser, Vitest and Playwright

steps.explanation: Each file owns exactly one role, which is why a command needs all five. `client.ts` is the sixth file in the picture but touches no command: it only chooses between the last two.

sources.why: The ipc/ folder's role in the architecture table.

steps.title: Why a hand-kept mock is a deliberate cost
steps.body: ADR 0007 chose an in-memory mock because Playwright cannot drive WebView2 or WebKitGTK, so the whole UI is tested against `createMockBackend`. The ADR states the consequence plainly: the mock must be kept in step with the Rust commands, since only the TypeScript interface and the generated event types are shared. That is why `mock/index.ts` reproduces Rust details such as the `NoRootOpen` and `IndexNotReady` rejections and generation numbers. Parity is a convention backed by tests, not by the compiler.

sources.why: What the mock is used for.

steps.title: Trace a command yourself
steps.instruction: Search the repo for `list_broken_links` and then for `listBrokenLinks`. Note which files show up for each spelling, and where both meet on one line of `src/ipc/tauri.ts`. Then check that every file you found is one of the five places from this chapter, plus the store and the panel that call it.
steps.expected: Snake_case in lib.rs, commands/graph.rs, tauri.ts and architecture.md; camelCase in types.ts, tauri.ts, the mock, the store and the panel.

sources.why: Both spellings meet on this line.

takeaways: A new command lives in five hand-synced places: commands/*.rs, the generate_handler! list in lib.rs, the Backend interface in ipc/types.ts, tauriBackend in ipc/tauri.ts and the mock in ipc/mock/index.ts, plus a store that calls it.
src/ipc/client.ts picks the implementation once, from __TAURI_INTERNALS__, so stores always import `backend` and never test the environment.
tsc catches a missing method on either implementation, but a missing lib.rs entry or a mistyped invoke string only fails at runtime in the real app.

chapters.title: The Rust side: a command in commands/ with AppState and AppError
chapters.goal: Write a #[tauri::command] in src-tauri/src/commands/graph.rs style: take State<AppState>, go through with_workspace so a closed folder yields NoRootOpen, return AppResult<T>, and register it in generate_handler! in lib.rs.

chapters.title: Types across the wire: ts-rs, camelCase and the generated folder
chapters.goal: Define a response struct with Serialize, TS, rename_all camelCase and #[ts(export)], explain how .cargo/config.toml (TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR, TS_RS_LARGE_INT) turns cargo test into the type generator, and why CI's git diff --exit-code on src/ipc/generated fails an unregenerated type.

chapters.title: The frontend contract: Backend interface and the Tauri implementation
chapters.goal: Add the method to the Backend interface in src/ipc/types.ts (import and re-export of the generated type), then implement it in tauri.ts through the wrapping invoke, with the camelCase argument names matching the Rust parameters, and explain how errors become BackendError.

chapters.title: The mock backend: behaving like Rust in src/ipc/mock
chapters.goal: Implement the command in createMockBackend (src/ipc/mock/index.ts) so it matches Rust: NoRootOpen rejection, the generation, state.graph/state.index readiness, structuredClone of results, and helper logic placed in a mock*.ts module; explain why the mock exists (ADR 0007).

chapters.title: Store and view: calling the command from the UI
chapters.goal: Call the new command from a zustand store action (as useGraph.loadBroken does, ignoring responses of an older generation) and render it in a view such as BrokenLinksPanel, and, when it is a user action, register it in menuActions.ts so menus, buttons and shortcuts dispatch through it.

chapters.title: Proving it: Rust tests, mock tests, Playwright and npm run check
chapters.goal: Test the command at each layer: a Rust unit test on a tempdir graph like commands/graph.rs, a Vitest test on createMockBackend after openRoot, a Playwright spec using openFixture and window.__igraspMock, then run npm run check and read what it covers.

chapters.title: Ship it: docs, changelog and the traps that remain
chapters.goal: Finish a command contribution the way IGrasp expects it: a row in docs/architecture.md's command table, the docs/features page, CHANGELOG [Unreleased], Conventional Commits; and list the drift risks (mock vs Rust, an unlisted handler, a filtered cargo test skipping export_bindings).
